LESSON 12 OF 106·Networking Fundamentals

Ports, Sockets and Common Services

What a port number is, how a socket pins one connection to one process, and why an unexpected listener on your machine is a security question rather than trivia.

Beginner2 min
Why this matters

A port is a number that identifies which service on a host should receive a connection. Knowing which ports carry which service is basic reconnaissance knowledge, and also basic defensive knowledge.

What you'll learn

By the end of this lesson you can:

  • list every listening port and the process behind it, not only the port
  • check which of those are reachable from outside the network you intended
  • notice management interfaces that share a host with a public service
  • compare the running services against what the system is actually needed for

How it works

  • A socket is one endpoint of a connection, made of an address, a port and a protocol.
  • Ports below 1024 are privileged on Unix-like systems, so binding them usually requires elevated privileges.
  • Well-known services have assigned ports, such as 22 for SSH, 53 for DNS, 80 and 443 for HTTP, and 389 for LDAP.
  • The service is often identified by port number, but real traffic carries a protocol, so a non-standard port can still be SSH.
  • A single exposed port can be the entry to a whole application, which is why port count is a reasonable proxy for attack surface.

The background

  • Ports came from the Berkeley socket interface in the early 1980s, which let one host run several distinct services at once.
  • The original assignment list was small and is now distributed by an Internet Assigned Numbers Authority registry.
  • Running services on non-standard ports was once a mild security measure, but it only reduces noise and is not a control.
  • Service naming and discovery moved to application layers, so ports today mostly describe transport rather than meaning.

Real-world examples

  • A database port reachable from outside the network is one of the most common serious misconfigurations found in practice.
  • Directory services exposed to the internet are a recurring target because they describe the whole organisation.
  • Running an administrative interface on a high port still leaves it fully discoverable by anyone scanning all ports.

What to look for

  • List every listening port and the process behind it, not only the port.
  • Check which of those are reachable from outside the network you intended.
  • Notice management interfaces that share a host with a public service.
  • Compare the running services against what the system is actually needed for.

Practice / apply

Use a suitable learning environment and follow the resource's instructions. Test other people's systems only with permission.

Key takeaways

  • Expose only what must be exposed, and reach everything else through an authenticated tunnel.
  • Keep management interfaces on a separate network from public traffic.
  • Remove services you no longer use, so there is nothing listening to find.
  • Baseline the listening ports and alert when the set changes.
